content:
This month, Google launched the all-new Pixel 11 series. Compared to last year's Pixel 10 series, the phones themselves haven't changed much, but there are some welcome improvements to the user experience, including a new camera processing option that gives users more granular control over the final look of their photos.

Hopefully, before the iPhone 18 Pro launches, Apple will add a similar feature.

Pixel 11 introduces a new camera feature called "Camera Looks," which is positioned somewhat like the iPhone's "Photographic Styles," letting users adjust how the camera processes images before they are taken. Because the adjustments are made before shooting, it's more than just a regular filter.

Like Apple, Google offers several preset styles, but goes a step further by letting users fine-tune each setting individually. Google has also added several new styles that fit the trends in modern smartphone photography, including Editorial, Velvet, Classic, Digi, Black Tie, and Minimal.

These styles are intentionally designed to move away from the heavily processed look common in smartphone photos, trying to recapture the feel of traditional photography. As the name suggests, the Digi style has limited dynamic range, high contrast, and gritty noise, producing results that look like they were shot on those compact point-and-shoot cameras from the 2010s.

Minimal, on the other hand, takes a completely low-processing approach, with most HDR processing turned off, making the final image much closer to what the phone's sensor actually captures. You can see some sample photos on the 9to5Google website.

Of course, shooting in ProRAW on iPhone can reduce post-processing to some extent, but doing so somewhat defeats the original purpose of using a phone to take photos.

Conclusion

If Apple wants to make a phone that can be pulled straight out of a pocket and capture the best possible shot, it must accept that every user has different needs. "Photographic Styles" is a good starting point, but Apple should go a step further. Photography is fundamentally a form of self-expression, so giving users more choices to decide how much post-processing their photos receive is an important step. Apple should take a page from Google and add a Minimal style to iPhone.

What do you think of iPhone's current photography performance? Do you like Apple's latest "Photographic Styles," or do you feel they still fall short? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
